Study Notes · Note 4

Business tax and the mayor's permit

Who pays the local business tax, how it is computed from last year's gross sales, when it is due, the penalties for paying late, and where the mayor's permit and the Business One Stop Shop fit in.

✓ Last checked: November 2026 · against RA 7160 (Local Government Code) and its amendments

Every January, the line at the municipal hall grows long with business owners renewing their permits. Two different things are paid at that time: the business tax, which is a tax on doing business, and the regulatory fees for the mayor's permit. This note explains both, using the Local Government Code (RA 7160) and the Ease of Doing Business Act (RA 11032).

Who may levy it

The business tax belongs to the municipality (Section 143). A city may levy the same taxes at rates up to 50% higher (Section 151), and so may municipalities in Metro Manila (Section 144). Barangays alone may tax small stores with gross sales of ₱50,000 or less in cities, or ₱30,000 or less in municipalities, at up to 1% (Section 152). The province has no general business tax, but it has its own taxes, such as those on printing and publication, franchises, amusement and delivery trucks (Note 1).

The tax base: last year's gross sales

The tax for this year is based on gross sales or receipts of the preceding calendar year. Gross sales means the total money received for goods or services, excluding discounts known at the time of sale, sales returns, excise tax and value-added tax (Section 131).

The rates in Section 143

Manufacturers, assemblers, repackers, processors, brewers, distillers

A fixed amount by bracket of gross sales; ₱6.5 million or more: up to 37.5% of 1%

Wholesalers, distributors, dealers

A fixed amount by bracket; ₱2 million or more: up to 50% of 1%

Exporters, and sellers of essential goods

Half the usual rates. Essential goods include rice and corn, flour, meat, dairy, sugar, salt, cooking oil and gas, laundry soap, detergents, medicine, farm inputs, feeds, school supplies and cement.

Retailers

2% of gross sales of ₱400,000 or less; 1% if more

Contractors

A fixed amount by bracket; ₱2 million or more: up to 50% of 1%

Banks and other financial institutions

Up to 50% of 1% of gross receipts from interest, commissions, discounts, leasing, dividends, rentals and similar

Peddlers

Up to ₱50 a year each

Any other business

A rate set by the sanggunian; no more than 2% for businesses subject to VAT, excise or percentage tax

Tip: As with every local tax, these are ceilings. The municipality's revenue code sets the actual schedule.

Rules that trip people up

  • Each establishment pays separately. One line of business does not become exempt because another line in the same place already pays (Section 146).
  • Two businesses with the same rate are taxed on their combined gross sales; businesses with different rates report their sales separately.
  • A branch or sales outlet records its own sales and pays where it is located (Section 150). For sales recorded in a principal office, 30% is taxed where the office is and 70% where the factory, plant, project office or plantation is.
  • A business that closes must file a sworn statement of its gross sales for the year and pay any balance before it is officially retired (Section 145).

When to pay, and the penalties

The tax period is the calendar year, and the tax may be paid quarterly (Section 165). It accrues on January 1; a new tax or a new rate starts on the first day of the next quarter after the ordinance takes effect (Section 166). Payment is due within the first 20 days of January, or of each quarter for those paying by installment. The sanggunian may extend this for a good reason, but by no more than six months (Section 167). If paid late, the sanggunian may impose a surcharge of up to 25% and interest of up to 2% a month on the tax plus surcharge, for no more than 36 months (Section 168).

The mayor's permit

Besides the tax, the municipality may charge reasonable fees for regulating, inspecting and licensing a business, but they must be commensurate with the cost of that work (Section 147). Before the permit is issued, the business needs a barangay clearance. The barangay must act on it within seven working days; if it does not, the city or municipality may issue the permit anyway (Section 152).

RA 11032 requires local governments to use a single unified business application form, to set up a Business One Stop Shop (BOSS), and to automate the process. Barangay clearances may now be issued at the city or municipal BOSS. Government offices must act on applications within three working days for simple transactions, seven for complex ones and twenty for highly technical ones, and an application not acted on in time is deemed approved.

Checking the books, and the taxpayer's remedies

The treasurer may examine a business's books once each tax period, during business hours, with a written authority if a deputy does it (Section 171). Unpaid taxes may be assessed within five years from the date they became due, or ten years from discovery of fraud (Section 194). A taxpayer who receives a notice of assessment may protest in writing within 60 days; the treasurer decides within 60 days, and the taxpayer has 30 days after a denial to go to court (Section 195). A refund claim must be filed with the treasurer, and no court case may be brought after two years from payment (Section 196).

Worked example: a sari-sari store that paid late

  1. A store in a municipality had gross sales of ₱300,000 last year. It is a retailer with sales of ₱400,000 or less, so the maximum rate is 2%.
  2. Annual business tax: ₱300,000 × 2% = ₱6,000, or ₱1,500 a quarter.
  3. The first-quarter installment was due January 20 but was paid on March 15.
  4. Surcharge at the maximum 25%: ₱1,500 × 25% = ₱375.
  5. Interest at 2% a month on the tax plus surcharge, for 2 months (January 21 to March 15, counting a part of a month as a month): (₱1,500 + ₱375) × 4% = ₱75.
  6. Amount due on March 15: ₱1,500 + ₱375 + ₱75 = ₱1,950.

Answer: Paying less than two months late raised the installment from ₱1,500 to ₱1,950. A store with sales of only ₱25,000 would instead pay the barangay, at up to 1%.

Practice

Tap your answer. A green ✓ means you got it right; a red ✗ means try to learn the right one, shown in green.

  1. What is the tax base of the municipal business tax?

    Show answer

    A. the gross sales or receipts of the preceding calendar year Section 143 bases the tax on gross sales or receipts of the preceding calendar year.

  2. What is the maximum rate on a retailer with gross sales of ₱400,000 or less?

    Show answer

    C. 2% Section 143(d): 2% for ₱400,000 or less, 1% if more.

  3. In a municipality, who may tax a store with gross sales of ₱25,000?

    Show answer

    D. the barangay Section 152: barangays alone may tax stores with sales of ₱30,000 or less in municipalities (₱50,000 or less in cities).

  4. Within what period must business taxes be paid?

    Show answer

    B. the first 20 days of January or of each quarter Section 167: within the first 20 days of January or of each subsequent quarter.

  5. What is the highest surcharge a sanggunian may impose on late business tax?

    Show answer

    C. 25% Section 168: a surcharge of up to 25%, plus interest of up to 2% a month for at most 36 months.

  6. A manufacturer records sales in its principal office in Makati but has its factory in a Quezon town. What share of those sales may the town tax?

    Show answer

    D. 70% Section 150(b): 30% to where the principal office is and 70% to where the factory is.

  7. Regulatory fees for the mayor's permit must be ____.

    Show answer

    D. commensurate with the cost of regulation, inspection and licensing Section 147: reasonable fees commensurate with the cost of regulation, inspection and licensing.

  8. If a barangay does not act on a clearance application within seven working days, what may happen?

    Show answer

    B. the city or municipality may issue the permit anyway Section 152(c): the city or municipality may issue the license or permit.

  9. How long does a taxpayer have to protest a notice of assessment for local taxes?

    Show answer

    C. 60 days Section 195: a written protest within 60 days of receiving the notice; the treasurer decides within 60 days.

  10. Under RA 11032, what is the processing time for a simple transaction?

    Show answer

    C. three working days RA 11032: three working days for simple, seven for complex and twenty for highly technical applications.

Laws and rules cited

  • Republic Act No. 7160, Local Government Code of 1991, Sections 131, 143 to 152 and 165 to 196
  • Republic Act No. 11032, Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018
